text: She made her name as a pioneer at Google, then as chief executive at Yahoo. Now Mayer is entering the crowded marketplace for A.I. assistants — and hoping to draw in more women with a product that tackles the mental load. Marissa Mayer has reinvented herself as a start-up founder, with a team of 10 engineers — a fraction of the armies of programmers she once commanded at Yahoo and Google. Credit... Kelsey McClellan for The New York Times Supported by By Alexandra Alter Reporting from Palo Alto Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer — the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer — likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers. So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect. Dazzle is a new consumer tech product from Mayer’s start-up, and her first push into the competitive marketplace for A.I. personal assistants. With Dazzle — which analyzes images in users’ camera rolls to answer questions, perform tasks and make suggestions — Mayer is aiming to build an A.I. tool that can handle everyday hassles, like buying a pair of pants you took a photo of, or finding a birthday present for your picky spouse. “A lot of what excites me is taking something that used to take you hours or minutes, and now getting it done in seconds,” Mayer told me at her company’s office in Palo Alto last month. Dazzle, which has been available since late September, harnesses information in users’ camera rolls to offer suggestions for their lives, like what to do on vacation or what to be for Halloween.
